blocks.2: The holly by the old town hall in the 1960s. Photo: From a brochure from the arboretum at Milde.
blocks.3: A brochure from the arboretum at Milde near Bergen says that the holly in Eivindvik (by the old town hall) is probably the largest holly in Scandinavia. It does not say when this was written, but it must be later than 1960, since the brochure contains some statistics up to that year. There is also a picture of the holly with a man leaning against the trunk. The holly has now broken down, but new shoots are coming up, so we may hope it can grow back to its “old heights”.
blocks.4: The 4 large spruces standing beside the holly were planted by Hans Sørensen Brandanger, probably in 1868–70. This was told by Hans's grandson, Håkon Brandanger. Hans worked for the priest one summer when he was very young. One day when they had been planting spruce in the parsonage outfield, Hans was given these plants by the priest. The priest said he could put the plants in the garden there for the time being and take them with him when he left in the autumn, but they stayed.
blocks.5: The fine oak by the bank building (the new building of 1978) is a gift to the bank from Marie Midttun, farm no. 19, holding no. 3. The plant was fetched from this holding and planted by the bank building by Stein Midtun (farm no. 15, holding no. 52), probably in 1984.
blocks.6: In the early 1970s a professor from Stockholm came here looking for filmy fern (Hymenophyllum). He had heard that this plant was to be found by the parsonage in Eivindvik. We did not find filmy fern while the professor was here, but later I found such a plant and sent it to Stockholm. The professor wrote back and said that this was the plant he had been looking for. I understood that it was a rather rare plant. The place where I found it was under the rock face west of Anne Karin and Geir Haveland's house.
blocks.8: Gangstadklubben is said to have got its name because people who came to church by boat walked up from there. This church path is also connected with Vetrestøa on Flolidstranda. I have heard that in winter, when Ilenessundet was frozen over, the churchgoers came ashore at Vetrestøa, walked from there overland to Midtunvågen, across the bay on the ice, and up again at Gangstadklubben. It is said that Vikings too came over Gangstadklubben when they were going to their gatherings in the area where the church now stands. From Gangstadklubben they walked out past where Sandal's house stands, over the fields where Ranghild Sognefest and Olav Midthun have their plots, and over the height where the church stands. Olav Midthun says that when he prepared his plot, there were clear signs that a road (path) had run there – in one place stones had been laid down to walk on.
blocks.9: Where Norstein's house stands was formerly called “Smedreset”, probably because the smith, Søren Larsen, had his workshop just below there.
blocks.10: The old village road from the steamer quay went up roughly where the doctors' surgeries are, past where Norstein's house is and through Sandal's farmyard – the house Åge Sandal now owns – and then on up through Skaret, over Haugane, through “Rauleet”, straight across Kristina and Fredrik Nerdahl's plot, over the outermost part of Grytelia, down again roughly at “Nyebrua” (the new bridge), and on into Midtunvågen along the same route as today. In really old days there was only a footpath from Midtunvågen to Eivindvik, and it went over Gryta and Stien and on through Grytelia above the rocks by the sea. It is probably this footpath, and perhaps also the parsonage having its path to the summer farm at Svartevatnet across the holding, that gave it the name Stien (the path).
blocks.11: Up and east of the steamer quay was called “Kleivane”, and in that area, people say, lived a woman called “Anne på Kleivane” and one known as “Pious Brit”. We all remember “Sørinastaua”, where “Storesørina” lived, and later (after the last world war) Tora Haugsdal.
blocks.12: In Oldrevika, at the bend at the junction where the road goes down to the steamer quay, there was a well with a water pump where boats could take on water.
blocks.13: Up at Skaret the young people of the village used to gather for fun. The area was formerly used as a showground for livestock.
blocks.14: The slope from Borgstova up towards Haugane was called Prestereina.
blocks.15: The “new” road from the parsonage, past the steamer quay and into Midtunvågen along the sea, was finished in 1924. It was built by the villagers, who paid a good part of the cost themselves. The stretch of road between “Gamlebanken” (the old bank, Jørs's house) and “Nyebrua” was called “the corkscrew” in everyday speech because of all its bends. “Nyebrua” (the new bridge) was called that to distinguish it from “Storebrua” (the big bridge) by the community hall. This bridge over the big river (the Midtun river) was the largest here before “Nyebrua” came. At Henriksbø we have “Jordmorbrua” (the midwife's bridge) over “Jordmorelva” (the midwife's river).
blocks.16: Beside the road, under the rock face just before Nyebrua, lay Martekjelda (Marte's spring). The water there was clear and good. The spring was surely named after “Marte i Urda”, whose house stood on the wall above the road by the old boathouse walls at Stien. Marte died in 1939, and the house was moved to Bremnes on Byrknesøy.
blocks.18: A settlement before Evindvik conciliation board of 4 November 1829, concerning the boundary between the parsonage and Gryta, says that Mikkelfjellet has also been called “Fløifjeld”. Olav H. Tveit also remembers old people talking about Fløyfjellet.
blocks.19: Some people believe that the name Mikkelfjellet may have come from St Michael. He was considered the chief of the angels and the special protector of Israel. He was to lead the righteous to Paradise, proclaim the resurrection with a horn signal and triumph in the last battle against Satan. In Europe Michael was considered the patron saint of soldiers and knights. He is also said to have been connected with seafarers. Masses in his honour were often held, it is said, in places from which one could look out over the sea, towards the ocean. St Michael was also called Sankte Mikkjel. His feast day was 29 September, Michaelmas. On the lowest part of Mikkelfjellet, where the terrain levels out, there could be plenty of room for a congregation. Perhaps this part of the mountain, because the Michaelmas masses were held there, was named after St Michael, and the name was then gradually used for the whole mountain?
blocks.20: Right at the front of Mikkelfjellet there used to be a stone cairn. Many in Eivindvik still remember this cairn. Gunhild Kversøy, Einar Navdal and Olav Midthun say that when they grew up here the cairn was about 100–150 cm high and about 1 m wide. It gradually shrank and finally disappeared completely.
blocks.21: People who have studied the old warning beacons believe that the cairn on Mikkelfjellet may be a remnant of the old chain of beacon watches leading to the Gulating. Of old beacons in this area that I have read about, Stemnebøveten, Neverdalsveten, Svabergveten and Midtunveten are mentioned. Where Midtunveten stood is not clear, but could it, even though this is now Gryta land, have been on Kvitefjellet? Rolf Midtun says he has seen stones that may be remains of such a cairn at the far west of Kvitefjellet by the old mountain path up Gudbrandskaret. Perhaps this mountain was called Vetefjellet (beacon mountain), and over time the name became Vitefjellet and changed to Kvitefjellet (white mountain). If Svabergveten had an “outpost” up on Svabergfjellet, as has been claimed, there is a clear line of sight from Mikkelfjellet to all these beacons (wherever the beacon stood on the mountains above Midtun) and down to Krossteigen. In addition, people in all of Eivindvik, including Midtunvågen, would see the signals from this cairn. There is also a good view out over the sounds and islands. One who has studied the old warning system closely is Oddkjell Bosheim, who now lives in Lærdal but is from Hallingdal. He says that with cairns in the places mentioned here, which he thinks very likely, the warning lines to and from Eivindvik seem very straightforward. Associate Professor Per Linge believes that the old system of beacon watches introduced in Norway by Håkon the Good was based on a Turkic warning system.
blocks.22: The mountain that many now want to call Kvitebergnova has always been called Høystakken (the haystack) here. That name used to be on the official maps too. On the oldest map I have seen of the area, the whole mountain range inland is named Midtunfjella, but on a map from 1866 (22D 10 and 11) there are names such as “Høiestakken”, “Braasviksaata”, “Ormekletten”, “Vatnestølen”, “Risestølen” and “Midtunstølen”.
blocks.23: In an on-site court case of 7 December 1797 concerning the boundary markers in the mountains here, “Høiestakken” also appears. This case concerns a boundary dispute between Gryta and Midtun, and it is then natural to believe that Høystakken must be Gryta or Midtun land, and so Kvitebergnova sounds even stranger to those of us who grew up here and know that the name of the mountain among the people here has been, and still is, Høystakken. From 1942 to 1946 a new map survey was carried out, and it seems that it was during this that the name was changed. I believe the new map came out in 1953. I have not seen any decision by Gulen municipality to change the name on the map.
blocks.25: The picture was probably taken in the 1920s. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.26: During the world war of 1914–18 the Western Norway Naval Command used Kjerringfjellet as a signal station. The purpose of the station was, as with other such stations along the coast, to watch for any foreign warships coming in towards the country. The naval command's journal also shows that meteorological observations were sent in.
blocks.27: The station on Kjerringfjellet was called “Sognefjord Signalstasjon”. I do not know when the hut that stood there was built, but in the naval command's archives at the State Archives in Bergen there is a copy of a letter of 21 June 1914 in which the signal foreman and signalmen are called up for a 3-week instruction course at Marineholmen, reporting on 20 July 1914, so the hut was probably put up in late winter and spring 1914. The signal foreman was the conscript sergeant Andreas Underthun, and the signalmen were Olav Nese (Henriksbø), Jørgen (Olsen) Midtun and Sigurd Larsen (Fonnevik). In 1916 Sigurd Larsen left (it seems because of poor health), and Jørgen (Ottesen) Midtun took his place.
blocks.28: In 1918 a “porch” was built onto the hut. The journal says (1 March 1918) that the bill for this extension has been paid at 288.77 kroner.
blocks.29: At the lookout post they had powerful binoculars, and a telephone was installed. People living on the coast reported to the watch if they spotted anything suspicious. Once a woman phoned and, quite shaken, reported that a submarine was on its way into the Sogn Sea. When the watch got their good binoculars on the “vessel”, it turned out to be a whale heading in. It was surely the spout of water the whale sent into the air that had aroused the woman's suspicion.
blocks.30: The weather up there could often be harsh. On the night of 8 October 1918 lightning struck and damaged the hut. The watchman (there was only one that night, Jørgen Ottesen Midtun) was knocked unconscious. The journal for 8 October 1918, journal no. 380, says: “telegr. Lightning strike on Sognefjorden. Temporarily without connection”, and no. 384, the same day: “report on the lightning strike”.
blocks.31: The station was dismantled in the spring of 1928. I have seen nothing in writing about when and to whom the hut was sold, but according to what people say it was Alfred Fosse (farm no. 20, holding no. 3) and Jon Midtun (farm no. 19, holding no. 1) who bought the hut. Later Jon Midtun was the sole owner. The hut was pulled down and the materials carried down to Midtun and later sold. The last thing carried down the mountain from the station was the bolt for a telescope stand. As a boy I was there when Jon blasted the bolt loose from the rock. Odd Midttun (Henriksbø) was there too. With sledgehammer and drill we drilled a hole in the rock next to the bolt, and it was blasted loose with dynamite. Jon was going to have it reforged into splitting wedges. I believe this happened in the early 1940s, during the last world war.
blocks.33: It was mentioned earlier that Kristian Hanssen was a driving force both in the youth society and in many other things. He was also an exceptionally good organist. Alongside his work as a teacher he was both parish clerk and organist in the church here until he left the village in 1946. His brother, Harald Hanssen, is said to have been an even greater talent in music. It is said that he played at services in the church when he was 11. He lived to be only 28, but in his short life he managed to give many concerts and delight many with his music. He also gave concerts here in the church; among other things he was here, together with Nan Dybdahl, on Sunday 8 July 1923, the same year he died. I have seen the printed programme for this concert; it still exists in the village. Harald and Kristian's father was also called Kristian Hanssen. He came here as a teacher from Domben in Solund.
blocks.35: It is said that once, while land was being cleared, a lump of gold was found at Gangstadklubben, under the rock face by Jørs's house.
blocks.36: Egil Undertun says, from his father Olav Undertun, that in the area where Eivindvik Stadion now lies, an archaeologist many years ago found remains showing that there had been a weapon smithy there in the saga age. The smithy lay under a rock face, roughly where the changing room building at the sports ground now stands.
blocks.37: In a cove on the west side of the Flolid farm lies a small plain. From what I have been told, both by people at Flolid and by others, this is the area that was called Vollane, and that is where they believe the old assembly field was.
blocks.38: Odd Midttun says that remains of 3 old tar kilns have been found at Henriksbø: 1 in Vassurda, 1 above Langeva and 1 in Sætråsmyra.
blocks.39: At Kattekletten, above Midtun, we used to see the remains of 2 stone huts, one on the lower and one on the upper Katteklettmyra. These huts had been used for hunting eagles. It is said that when the farmer on farm no. 20, holding no. 1 was going to shoot eagles, he and his wife went into the hut together under a blanket. The wife then went out and home again, while the husband stayed lying there waiting for the eagle. Going in together under the blanket was to trick the eagle: it saw one go in and one come out, and then thought the hut was empty and that it was free to help itself to the bait. Whether this trick led to many eagles being shot I do not know.
blocks.40: As mentioned earlier, the parsonage had a summer farm at Henriksbø in older times. Gryta was the widow's seat for the priests' widows until well into the last century. (I have also seen Vesøyna mentioned in connection with Gryta; perhaps the priests' widows had grazing rights there?)
blocks.41: I have heard the stream east of the old people's home called “Kvernhusbekken” (the mill-house brook). There must have been a mill house for the parsonage there.
blocks.42: There was also a place for washing clothes by the stream. Olav H. Tveit remembers that the people at Stølen boiled and washed clothes there by the stream. They also had clotheslines there; it was a particularly good drying place.
blocks.43: The small barn on Haukøya used to stand as a retirement cottage at Grønevika.
blocks.44: It looks as if Midtun was the oldest independent farm in Midtunvågen (the farmyard between two parts of what belonged to the farm where the parsonage now lies). That the bay is named after Midtun would also suggest that this was the oldest and largest farm at the head of the fjord here. Old people said that the farmers at Midtun in earlier times used Gryta as a calf paddock. As a sign that this may be right, it is pointed out that the stone wall on the boundary between the infields of Gryta and Midtun is called Sjølegarden, the wall with the gate down to the sea (where the calves went), while the wall in the outfields is called Grytegarden, which came after Gryta had become a holding of its own.
blocks.45: On farm no. 20, holding no. 3 at Midtun there stood an old cowshed that in older times had been a smoke-hole house and dwelling on the farm. This house is said to have stood there before the holding was separated (from holding no. 2) as a holding of its own, and it is claimed that the house was several hundred years old. The house was pulled down in 1988 when the new farm building was built.
blocks.46: Ole J. Midtun has told, from his grandfather, that during the cholera epidemic of 1849–50 victims were buried in the bog below Kleivhamaren. Because of the great risk of infection, those who died in the epidemic were buried as soon as possible, and we have several examples of this happening outside consecrated burial grounds too.
blocks.47: By the road up to Kleivhamaren lay a reddish stone; it was called Rausteinen (the red stone) and has now been built into the new road.
blocks.48: It is said that Lindesteinen on Langhogen turned round when the church bells rang.
blocks.49: In an article in “Budstikken” in 1824, Dean Dahl writes that duels (holmgang) are said to have been fought on Timmerøya and that the island is said to have been a place of execution and a burial place for the executed and for people who took their own lives.
blocks.50: The former croft north-east of Grønevika has been called Soleibotn. It has been claimed that the name comes from the plant soleie (buttercup). People who grew up in the area believe that the background for the name is not buttercup but sun – the hollow by the sunny slope, or the hollow with lots of sun in it. Older maps and documents support this. Olav Tveit (at Stølen) says that when his parents got the title deed for the holding Stølen, probably in 1928, Sollibotn was also mentioned, and Olav, who has also seen the documents since, remembers that the name was written with li and not lei. In the consolidation document dated 27 August 1954 it says “Sollibotn”. On an old map from about 1800 the name is written “Solliebotten”, and on a map from 1860 there is “Solibot..”, the rest of the name missing. In a list of death certificates of 8 November 1892, signed by the parish priest Sandberg, it says “Solibotnen”. The spelling of the name was taken up for reconsideration in 1994, and in 1995 the municipal council decided that the name is again to be written Sollibotn.
blocks.52: The first motor vehicle to come to our village was a small lorry, a 1938-model “Fargo”, which Odd Midttun bought in 1951. The first car came in 1956. It belonged to the district doctor Fischer. I do not know what make and model it was. At that time there was no road connection out of Eivindvik.
blocks.53: It is said that Gunnar Henriksbø, farm no. 21, holding no. 7, who was exceptionally good at rock work and worked as a foreman for many years, holds the European record for tunnel drilling.
blocks.54: In 1904 Eivindvik got a telephone exchange; it was probably already then in Peder Sandal's house (farm no. 15, holding no. 4). The exchange stayed on this property right up until it was closed when the telephone was automated in 1984.
blocks.55: The first radio receiver belonged to the ship's captain Johannes Norstein; he built it himself. He also became the first owner of a television set here when NRK started television broadcasts around 1960. After he retired as a ship's master with Fylkesbaatane in 1955, on reaching the age limit, he worked installing television aerials for people. He took out a patent on a “winch device” that was used, among other places, on Fylkesbaatane's boats. I know that he also went to Copenhagen to help install the winch device on a newbuilding at a yard there.
blocks.56: The youth society's paper for 6 November 1927 says that that year we got a new priest, a new doctor, a new parish clerk and a newly married sheriff – quite an eventful year.
blocks.58: An old broadside ballad that was widely known has a connection with Eivindvik. It was probably made here. An assistant priest, Peter Bugge, fell in love with one of the priest's daughters. They were apparently even engaged, but then the relationship fell apart. He was deeply disappointed, felt betrayed and let his feelings find expression in a song. The song was written in the second half of the last century. Staff at Bergen library have obtained the song for me, noted down by someone who remembered it. According to the note it goes like this (translated from the Dano-Norwegian):

blocks.103: Here in Eivindvik too we have had people who were good at coming up with quick answers and reactions. I recall the following:
blocks.104: At a wedding with guests from both Masfjorden and Gulen, some got rather “wet”. The priest was also a guest at the wedding, and some who thought things were going a bit far spoke to the priest and said they were sorry about the situation. “Well, I can see that the people of Gulen hold their drink better than the people of Masfjorden”, said the priest.
blocks.105: Once when a temperance meeting was to be held in the old town hall, only a few turned up, among them the priest. When the meeting was cancelled, the priest is supposed to have said: “Now we'll go to the parsonage and have a glass of wine”.
blocks.106: The parish clerk was also at the meeting. He was a good rhymester, and on the way up to the parsonage he made up a rhyme about the situation. Unfortunately I do not know how the rhyme went, but it was something about “the thirsty crowd” heading off to the spring.
blocks.107: From the war years, another priest, when there was a great shortage of tobacco: on board the ferry boat the boatman took out his tobacco, rolled himself a cigarette and lit it. The priest watched and said: “Now I've stopped smoking”. “Oh, and when did you stop?” “Yesterday”. The boatman understood the situation, and the priest got a welcome “fill” for his pipe.
blocks.108: One year the boatman had made his boat available to some people who rigged up a kind of “harpoon” on it. They apparently also tried to catch a sturgeon with this gear, but it did not go so well. The following spring the priest said to the boatman: “Are you going sturgeon fishing this year?”
blocks.109: Also told of the same priest: the priest was, as usual at that time, chairman of the school board and received many complaints about school transport. One of the district chairmen said: “Yes, it's so bad that we could have been lost at sea several times.” “Oh, it would probably only have been once”, was the priest's comment.
blocks.110: The priest was a keen participant in events in the village. At a Mother's Day party the question came up of which song to sing. “Perhaps ‘Kjerringa med staven’ (The old woman with the stick) would suit”, said the priest.
blocks.111: A little boy was out with his father one fine moonlit evening. It was during the war. When his father said the moon was only half tonight, the little boy took it to mean that if the moon was no longer whole, something must be wrong, and he said: “It wasn't me who broke the moon; it must be the Germans who shot it to pieces”.
blocks.112: A boatman had a passenger in his boat who was not used to the sea. The boatman was what we call pocket-familiar with the waters and kept close to land. The passenger was clearly afraid they would hit a “rock”, and in the end he could not hold back any longer: “There's sea on the other side too, you know”, he hissed.
blocks.113: On a very hot summer's day a man came puffing and panting up to a neighbour. As the man wiped the sweat and complained about the heat, he said: “Goodness me, how hot it is”. “Put it in water, then”, came the prompt reply from the neighbour.
blocks.114: A sheriff was out fishing with his farmhand. They caught nothing, and they complained about this when the neighbour, the parish clerk and cantor, rowed past. The parish clerk threw two small cod into the sheriff's boat, saying: “Here are two cod (toskar – also meaning fools), and with the two of you already there, that makes a suitable whist party.”
blocks.115: Two men, both known for liking a glass of wine or two, sat at a table telling stories to each other. They seemed to be having a great time. Someone at the next table said: "Now they're lying each other so drunk that they'll have to help each other out."
blocks.116: A farmer was hauling shell sand from Sunndalsbrygga home to his farm. Someone he met on the road said: “You're hauling big loads; it'll be heavy for the horse.” “Yes,” the farmer answered, “I don't understand how he manages it”.
blocks.117: Once when some farmers were burning off scrub, they could not control the fire. Many people gathered to help put it out, but it looked bad. When the sheriff came and saw how things stood, he said: “You should all be put in the lock-up, the whole gang of you”. One of the men answered instantly: “Well, we'd damn well better put the fire out first”.
blocks.118: Another time this man sat with a number of others in a neighbour's living room chatting. A trumpet lay on the table. One of those present took the trumpet and got a few awful noises out of it. “Yes, you can tell when experienced people get hold of it”, said the man. A little later the person who had blown the trumpet tried the instrument again, but the “music” was no more successful this time. “Yes, I can hear you've had a go at it before”, was the comment now.
blocks.119: An elderly mayor had become somewhat “forgetful”, as many do in their old age. The man mentioned before had seen the mayor on the road one day. When he met some men at the shop, he asked: “Is there a council meeting today?” The answer was yes. “I thought so; I met a man with a loose head down the road.”
blocks.120: An elderly lady who was considered a little “posh” was talking with the man, and the conversation turned to funeral customs. “I think I want to be buried”, said the lady. “You can be sure they will”, he answered. “My sister, she was cremated”. The man cleared his throat: “Yes, that was probably the safest”.
blocks.121: The man did a bit of painting for people. One of the farmers here renovated a small bedroom and painted the walls blue. He let the man see the result of his work. The man stood for a while and then said: “I'll tell you what, scrape that off again and I'll fix it”.”
blocks.122: Perhaps the comment on what I have now written would be somewhat in the same vein, but it will have to stand as it is. Thank you for reading it!
